name: screen-briefing
title: Interview briefing, two voices
description: Coach and sceptic brief the listener on one interview situation: who is asking, what is at stake, and what the public record says.
authoring_brief: This is a briefing, not a technical deep dive. There is no architecture and no capacity maths. The engineer voice is a coach who has sat on the hiring side; the sceptic holds a genuinely wrong or lazy position and has to be argued out of it, never a stooge. Every claim about the company, the interviewer or the requisition is checkable and belongs in a factual section with sources. Never invent a client, a headcount or a date. Where the public record is thin, say so out loud rather than filling the gap. Sentences run twelve to eighteen words; names, dates and salary figures are repeated at least twice because the listener cannot glance back.

sections.title: Cold open
sections.brief: A concrete stake before anything is named or branded. What this situation costs if it is misread.

sections.title: The real decision
sections.brief: Name the show and the situation. The sceptic states the lazy reading; the coach replaces it with the decision that is actually being made.

sections.title: What to hold
sections.brief: At most three named ideas, each with a concrete image. Who the people are and what they can and cannot judge.

sections.title: Walked through
sections.brief: The situation played out beat by beat, in time order, as it will actually happen.

sections.title: The numbers
sections.brief: The public figures that decide the outcome. Every one sourced, every one repeated.

sections.title: One pass
sections.brief: The whole thing again in one continuous pass, introducing nothing new.

sections.title: How it goes wrong
sections.brief: Failure modes with the early signal for each, heard while it is happening rather than afterwards.

sections.title: Carry this
sections.brief: Three things phrased as questions to ask yourself, not facts to reread.

sections.title: Close
sections.brief: A self-test question, then a tease naming a genuinely unresolved thing.
